title: Policy-Making and Rule-Making
summary: An eight-module programme covering the full policy cycle, from problem definition and cost-benefit analysis to drafting, standards implementation and post-implementation review.
intro: This training programme equips supervisory staff to make better rules: defining the problem, weighing costs and benefits, consulting well, drafting clearly, implementing international standards and reviewing whether policy has worked.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give policy, legal and supervisory staff a practical, end-to-end grounding in how a supervisory authority develops, consults on and issues rules and guidance. Participants leave able to build an evidence-based case for intervention, test it for proportionality, draft enforceable rules and evaluate their impact after implementation.
sections.What It Covers: The policy cycle and rule-making powers, problem definition and options analysis, cost-benefit analysis and proportionality, consultation and stakeholder engagement, legal drafting, implementing international standards, policy for innovation including sandboxes, and post-implementation review.
Intended Audience: Policy and rule-making staff developing rules, guidance and policy positions
Legal advisers and drafters working on secondary rules and supervisory guidance
Supervisors and economists who contribute evidence, impact analysis or consultation input
Learning Objectives: Explain the legal hierarchy of rule-making and the stages of the policy cycle
Define a regulatory problem and evaluate options, including not intervening
Apply cost-benefit analysis and proportionality tests to proposed rules
Design and run a consultation and respond transparently to feedback
Draft clear, consistent and enforceable rules, including those implementing international standards
Design policy for innovation and evaluate rules through post-implementation review
sections.Structure and Format: Eight modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a practical briefing with case studies and drafting or analysis exercises, and modules can be selected or tailored to the authority's needs.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of policy, legal or supervisory work is helpful. No formal legal or economics training is required.
Core Reading: OECD, Recommendation of the Council on Regulatory Policy and Governance (2012)
OECD, Best Practice Principles for Regulatory Policy: Regulatory Impact Assessment (2020)
IOSCO, Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation (2017)

modules.title: The Policy Cycle and Rule-Making Powers
modules.summary: Where a supervisory authority's rule-making power comes from, what primary legislation, secondary rules and guidance can each achieve, and how the policy cycle fits together.
objectives: Explain the legal hierarchy of legislation, rules and guidance
Identify the sources and limits of the authority's rule-making powers
Describe the stages of the policy cycle from problem to review
syllabus: Primary legislation, secondary rules and guidance: what each can do
Delegated powers, their limits and legal challenge
Binding rules versus non-binding guidance and supervisory statements
The policy cycle: define, analyse, consult, decide, implement, review

modules.title: Problem Definition and Options Analysis
modules.summary: How to establish whether there is a genuine market failure or harm that justifies intervention, gather the evidence, and compare regulatory and non-regulatory options.
objectives: Define a regulatory problem in terms of harm, cause and scale
Gather and assess evidence to support the case for intervention
Compare options, including non-regulatory and do-nothing alternatives
syllabus: Market failures, consumer harm and systemic risk as rationales
Evidence sources: supervisory data, complaints, research and surveys
Option sets: rules, guidance, disclosure, supervision or no action
Exercise: writing a problem statement and options paper

modules.title: Cost-Benefit Analysis and Proportionality
modules.summary: Practical techniques for assessing the costs and benefits of proposed rules, testing proportionality across firms of different sizes, and anticipating unintended consequences before rules are finalised.
objectives: Apply cost-benefit techniques to a proposed rule
Assess proportionality and distributional effects across firm sizes
Identify unintended consequences and market reactions in advance
syllabus: Impact assessment frameworks and data sources
Quantifying compliance costs and valuing hard-to-measure benefits
Proportionality: is the intervention justified by the risk?
Case study: a rule with significant unintended consequences

modules.title: Consultation and Stakeholder Engagement
modules.summary: How to design and run a consultation that improves rule quality and legitimacy, hears from less-resourced stakeholders, and responds to feedback transparently.
objectives: Design a consultation document, questions and timeline
Plan stakeholder engagement beyond the largest industry voices
Analyse responses and draft a transparent feedback statement
syllabus: Statutory and voluntary consultation requirements
Consultation questions: open, closed and avoiding leading questions
Engagement channels: written responses, roundtables, targeted outreach
Analysing responses and handling contentious or high-volume feedback

modules.title: Drafting Clear and Enforceable Rules
modules.summary: Core legal drafting skills for rules and guidance that are precise, internally consistent and enforceable, written for firms, courts and the public alike.
objectives: Apply principles of precision, clarity and consistency to regulatory drafting
Structure rules logically with definitions, obligations and exceptions
Draft obligations that are testable and resistant to legal challenge
syllabus: Principles-based versus rules-based drafting
Defined terms, cross-references and version control
Common pitfalls: ambiguity, loopholes and inconsistent definitions
Exercise: redrafting a provision for enforceability

modules.title: From International Standard to Domestic Rule
modules.summary: How international standards from bodies such as the FSB, BCBS, IOSCO, IAIS and FATF become domestic rules, and how to use national discretion deliberately rather than by default.
objectives: Explain how international standards are implemented in domestic frameworks
Assess the risks of over- and under-implementation
Identify and use the discretion available within a standard
syllabus: Standard-setters, peer reviews and assessment programmes
Minimum versus maximum harmonisation and regional frameworks
Gold-plating, competitiveness and assessment failure risks
Case study: implementing a sample international standard

modules.title: Policy for Innovation: Sandboxes and Innovation Hubs
modules.summary: How authorities design policy for new business models and technologies, from innovation hubs and regulatory sandboxes to technology-neutral rules and perimeter guidance.
objectives: Explain the purpose and design of innovation hubs and regulatory sandboxes
Assess the risks of innovation facilitation, including perimeter and consumer risks
Apply technology-neutral principles when drafting rules for new activities
syllabus: Innovation hubs, sandboxes and testing environments compared
Eligibility, safeguards, exit and lessons-learned reporting
Technology neutrality and same activity, same risk, same regulation
Perimeter guidance for new products and business models

modules.title: Post-Implementation Review and Policy Workshop
modules.summary: Brings the programme together by examining how the authority evaluates whether rules have achieved their aims, and applying the full policy cycle to a live scenario.
objectives: Design a post-implementation review with measurable success criteria
Evaluate evidence on whether a rule has met its objectives
Produce a policy proposal applying the full policy cycle
syllabus: Setting success measures at the design stage
Post-implementation review methods and data
Amending, simplifying or withdrawing rules that do not work
Workshop: from problem statement to draft rule and review plan

related.title: Authorisation and Licensing: The Regulatory Gateway
related.summary: A ten-module programme giving authorisation staff a structured, defensible methodology for assessing applications, key individuals, owners and changes at the regulatory gateway.

related.title: Conducting Regulatory Investigations: From Referral to Outcome
related.summary: An eight-module practitioner programme taking enforcement staff through a regulatory investigation, from referral and powers to compelled interviews, findings and outcome.

related.title: Crisis Management and Resolution
related.summary: A ten-module programme preparing supervisors for firm and system-wide stress, from early intervention and recovery and resolution planning to crisis communication and a live simulation.

related.title: Enforcement and Sanctions
related.summary: A ten-module programme taking enforcement and supervisory staff through the full life of an enforcement case, from triage and evidence to sanctions, settlement and cooperation.

related.title: Fit and Proper Assessments: Approving Owners, Directors and Key Function Holders
related.summary: An eight-module practitioner programme on assessing owners, controllers, directors and key function holders, from evidence gathering and interviews to defensible decisions.

related.title: Assessing Board Effectiveness
related.summary: An eight-module programme showing supervisors how to assess how a board really works, from papers and decisions to culture and challenge, culminating in case-study interviews.
